said:
What affects people
In Port Vesper, safety, trust and available resources are closely connected. A missing technician may simultaneously be a personal tragedy, a search operation and a maintenance problem.
An event has consequences when someone witnesses it, hears about it reliably or a system records it. Not everyone immediately knows what happened.
| Event | First response | Possible further consequences |
| Someone misses an agreed check-in | The watch tries to make contact and checks the destination, route and last sighting. | A search, postponed work and concern among acquaintances. |
| Serious injury or a distress signal | The watch calls Edda and organises safe retrieval. | Medical supplies are consumed; someone takes over work; recovery may interrupt appointments. |
| A confirmed death | Those close to the deceased are informed personally. Identity and circumstances are recorded. | A wake, a place in the Harbour Record and a lasting change in duties and relationships. |
| Theft or missing materials | The person in charge checks issues, counts and possible mistakes. | A search for witnesses and traces; missing parts may delay a repair. |
| An ongoing shortage | The person in charge explains what is scarce and what it is needed for. | Orders, replacement parts, voluntary collection or limited rationing. |
| A dangerous malfunction | The relevant installation or route is cordoned off. | A repair assignment, changed schedules and investigation of the cause. |
| Someone leaves | Duties, borrowed items and outstanding commitments are handed over. | An empty workplace, new responsibilities and possibly messages from far away. |
| An important repair succeeds | The installation is checked and released for use again. | Work resumes, tension eases and those involved acknowledge the contribution. |
| A new signal anomaly | Preserve the recording, check measuring equipment and seek a second observation. | A research appointment or adjusted expedition preparation; no immediate general panic. |

Customs and customary aftermath
A disappearance The Return Check
Anyone travelling alone to Orison reports a destination and expected check-in time. If that time passes, the first step is to try making contact. A brief delay does not yet mean someone is missing.
When a check-in is thirty minutes overdue, contact repeatedly fails or a specific alarm is raised, the watch assesses the situation. A search team sets out with appropriate equipment. Bad weather may require a different approach; nobody is sent after a missing person without assessment.
The player can help search, operate the radio, provide materials or take over work. A reasonable rescue attempt is made even without the player.
A death Holding the Name
As long as medical recovery remains possible, residents speak of a rescue or critical condition. Remembrance follows only after irreversible death is confirmed.
At the next appropriate evening meal, one chair remains empty. Acquaintances share a memory; Sana preserves a personal message in the Harbour Record. A memorial plaque remains on a designated wall in Commons.
For a disappearance without a confirmed outcome, a pending return marker is displayed. It is not changed into a death notice without evidence.
A shortage Open Stores
Mara and the relevant person in charge publish a short stock notice: what is missing, what it is needed for and what alternatives exist. Residents can lend parts or offer labour.
A voluntary contribution remains voluntary. Emergency reserves are released only according to established authority. A completed collection or restored supply is also announced, so concern does not persist indefinitely.
Departure and safe return
On departure, a person hands over their work and outstanding obligations. On return, an acquaintance asks what happened along the way. A dangerous journey that ends well may prompt a shared meal; not every departure receives a ceremony.
Dangers in the initial play area
The first phase has no hostile alien civilisation and no roaming monsters. The main dangers are understandable and fit Nacre.
| Danger | What may happen | Possible approach |
| Storms cold and poor visibility | Hypothermia, getting lost, falling material or slipping. | Prepare, shelter, turn back, escort or rescue. This is not a hit-point battle. |
| Electrical and mechanical faults | A damaged cable, moving machine or faulty closure may cause injury. | Isolate power, keep a distance, call qualified staff or carry out a controlled repair. |
| Faulty maintenance drone | A machine follows an incorrect work order and blocks or damages a passage. | Stop it remotely, cut its power, restrain it or, as a last resort, physically disable it. |
| Territorial coastal animals | An animal defends a nest or feeding area beside a route. | Keep a distance, take a detour or drive it away with appropriate equipment. Attacking is possible but usually unnecessary. |
| Human conflict | An argument over supplies, access or suspected sabotage may escalate. | Talk, bring witnesses, step away, protect someone or intervene in immediate danger. |

The coastal animals are provisionally called sailbacks: low, six-legged animals with a ribbed dorsal crest. They feed on native organisms in the tidal zone, are not edible for humans and do not hunt them. Their presence near a path is signalled by tracks, sounds or visible threatening behaviour.
A maintenance drone is a specialised tool, not an independently malevolent AI. A fault has an established cause. Not every malfunction turns out to be sabotage.
Who responds to your actions
There is no general reputation reward for “defeating an enemy”. People judge necessity, proportionality, damage and what they know about it.
| Party | What matters to them |
| Vesper Maintenance Cooperative | Safe shutdown, preserving usable equipment and reporting the cause. Unnecessarily destroying a drone causes damage for which you may be held responsible. |
| Settlement Marshal and harbour watch | Protecting people, preserving evidence and handing over suspects without unnecessary violence. Suspicion does not give the player an unlimited right to detain someone. |
| Peregrine Expedition Crew | Acting reliably under pressure. Reckless violence may be grounds to reconsider your role or participation. |
| The Keeping Circle | Helping the injured, respecting the dead and caring for those left behind. Someone who committed an offence may still need help. |
| Researchers and local residents | Avoiding unnecessary damage to the ecosystem. Killing a sailback in immediate self-defence is judged differently from killing animals for entertainment. |

Paying handing over or letting go
Paying: compensation, a fine or an agreed settlement may resolve a conflict. Paying someone who threatens you buys, at most, temporary safety; it does not make extortion lawful.
Handing over: in the case of a specific dangerous offence, the player can help the watch escort someone safely. The authorised people then investigate and decide.
Letting go: allowing someone to leave after de-escalation may be wise. Punishing a helpless person does not automatically earn approval.
Defeating: the end of a fight records who was injured, fled or surrendered. Witnesses and those involved respond to that outcome; not everyone receives the same information.
For the Chronicler
Give dangers recognisable warning signs beforehand. A quiet route usually remains quiet. Repeated journeys must not be interrupted by a random fight every time.
New dangers may later appear at Echo Nine, but establish their behaviour and limits before using them. Unknown does not automatically mean hostile.
Every important event must be able to answer three questions: who noticed it, who acts on it and what trace remains?

{"say":"Here is a first set of signals and customs for Port Vesper. I kept to what the engine can actually see.

**Signals and their customs**
- **A death** leads to Holding the Name: grief over the area, one empty chair at the next evening meal in the Commons, a new plaque on the memorial wall, and a Harbour Record entry told as news.
- **A theft or missing materials** leads to a recount, then word carried to Mara. Nobody is accused by custom.
- **A lasting shortage** leads to Open Stores: a stock notice, Mara weighing up the reserves, prices up a little for five days, and a closing notice about a week later so the worry does not run on for ever.
- **Violence between residents** leads to a threat mood, a thought for the injured, and Mara offering to mediate after a day.
- **A house left empty** (someone has gone) leads to the neighbours thinking about the duties and borrowed things still outstanding, and a quiet line of news.
- **A danger that is past** (belief: the danger is back to normal) leads to a brief easing mood, prices down slightly, and a telling of the rescue that grows with each teller.
- **made_good** (the engine sends it when a broken word is made good) leads to a thought for the person owed and a mug kept by the urn in the Commons for the stranger.

**Creatures and encounters**
- **The sailback** is a beast that warns before it strikes and flees early. It belongs to no faction. Killing one costs 2 with the Peregrine crew, and driving it off earns 1 with them.
- **A faulty maintenance drone** belongs to the Maintenance Cooperative. Stopping it gains 2 and restraining it gains 3; wrecking it loses 8. The engine's creature kinds have nothing for machines, so it is listed as 'beast'. That only affects fight rules, not how it is told.
- Both encounters sit on the Coastal Service Path, are rare, and wait at least a week before they can happen again. Storms, cold and faulty gear are not fights here.

**Assumptions to check in the builder**
- I assumed the engine records deaths, thefts and violence as facts of kind death, theft and assault; assault is the word the law already uses.
- I have left out the Return Check, a signal anomaly and a successful repair.
